text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended higher in thin activity. September added $5 to close at $1,515 per tonne while November closed $4 higher at $1,530 per tonne. The nearby spread remains at a discount with spot September weighed down by ample supply.

Arabica futures in New York attempted to rally but could not find much buying interest. September closed 1.45 cents/lb higher at 184.55 cents/lb, while December added 55 points to close at 166.05 cents/lb. Trade buying of the nearby switches helped to steady the market.

The focus is on Friday's release of the GCA stock figures and there was talk of an increase of between 100,000 to 200,000 bags in July. Traders said the most transparent aspect of analyzing the GCA data regards CSCE certified stocks, which are included in the total. Although certified stock levels remain low, there was an increase from 49,825 bags on July 1 to 92,120 bags on August 13, according to CSCE data.

Perhaps more significant to the GCA figure than certified levels of washed arabica coffee is the level of imports of Brazilian unwashed arabicas and robustas, however. An increase in shipment of these types of coffee to the United States in recent months has been a major factor in the GCA stock rise. Moreover, rumors have circulated again that sizeable amounts of robusta coffee have been shipped to the United States from Europe or Africa by some trade-houses, which could have an impact on the GCA data.

Another factor, probably pointing to higher GCA stock figures is a slight shift in the buying strategy of roasters. The sharp reduction in stock levels in previous years was mainly due to roasters in the United States and Europe adopting a 'just in time-JIT-'buying strategy to reduce running costs. But concern about supplies of mild arabica coffee and a sharp price rise earlier this year signalled that industry stocks had become too lean and levels have since been increased. Moreover, the sharp rise in exports, as reported by the ICO, suggests that there was an increase in stocks in consumer hands.
UNITED STATES - The CSCE reported certified coffee stocks fell by 839 bags as of August 13 to 92,120 bags. There were no bags pending grading.

BRAZIL - Brazilian industry sources warned that the sharp drop in coffee received by co-operatives in past months is proof that this year's crop will show a significant fall from the 1996/97 figure. The 1996/97 crop is generally believed to have been between 25 to 28 million bags.

Recently, the CNC said that 1.16 million bags of coffee had been received by co-operatives during July, bringing the total since May to 1.96 million bags. This is down 30 per cent from the 28.0 million bags delivered in the same period in 1996. Estimates for the 1997/98 Brazilian crop range between 18 to 28 million bags, with the USDA plotting the current harvest as slightly higher than the 27.5 million bags it estimated was harvested in 1996/97. The government is working with a figure of 24 million bags while traders in Brazil believe the crop could be around 24 million bags.

Exports of green coffee in 1997/98 are forecast at 15 million bags (allowing for Brazil being given the same export allowance at an upcoming meeting of the ACPC) while exports of solubles could be around 2.2 million bags. Internal demand in 1997/98 is estimated at 11.5 million bags yielding total requirements of 28.7 million bags.

If production should be around 24 million bags then there would be a gap of 4.7 million bags which would have to be covered by sales of government stocks estimated at 12.19 million bags. Recently the Sao Paulo State Coffee Industry Union once again called on the government to increase the size of its monthly sales to ease current supply problems for domestic roasters.

SOUTH KOREA - South Korea imported 201,200 bags of coffee in January/February 1997, 27 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 dropped by 8 per cent to 995,500 bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/February 1997 were Brazil (21,500 vs 23,600 bags), Colombia (21,700 vs 28,000 bags), Indonesia (54,900 vs 57,100 bags) and Vietnam (25,200 vs 8,400 bags).

ROMANIA - Romania imported 61,000 bags of coffee in January/March 1997, 16 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1996. Total imports in calendar year 1996 soared to 467,200 bags, from 243,200 bags imported the previous year. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/March 1997 were Brazil (10,600 vs 17,200 bags) and Indonesia (35,500 vs 37,100 bags).
